body: For oil, a Trump, Xi and Putin meeting focused partly on ending the Iran war is a potential de-escalation catalyst. It sits awkwardly with Rubio’s assessment that talks with Tehran are not productive and with the weekend’s strikes on regional energy infrastructure , so crude is likely to treat it as a headline to watch rather than a reason to reprice. For Nvidia, Trump’s backing offers some cushion ahead of tonight’s first session since Huang’s admission , though his “you never know” caveat stops short of a full endorsement. Whether Huang is on the trip will be read as a signal of his standing on China chip policy. Trump is heading to China with Iran and nuclear arms on the agenda for possible talks with Xi and Putin, and he says he would gladly bring Jensen Huang along, a show of support that could become a test of Huang’s political standing. US President Donald Trump said he expects to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at next week’s APEC summit in China. He also said he would be willing to take Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang on the trip, despite the controversy over Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said a meeting with Xi and Putin “will be interesting” and would cover a lot of ground, including denuclearisation and ending the war in Iran, Reuters reported. Such a meeting would bring the leaders of the US, China and Russia together as the Iran conflict grinds through its eighth month. On Huang, Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia chief about the allegations but described him as a fine and honourable person who had done an amazing job for the United States. He added that Huang probably had an explanation and that it should be heard, while acknowledging that “you never know what is going on.” Asked whether Huang would join him in Asia, Trump said he did not know but would certainly take him. Trump’s remarks came on the same day that Huang admitted to a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom US officials reportedly believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, and that Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation. The board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and Huang remains chief executive. Whether Huang travels to China alongside the president will be closely watched. His presence would signal that the White House still sees him as a key voice on AI and chip policy. His absence would suggest the affair has begun to cost him political access at a sensitive moment for US export controls. In a lighter moment, Trump said he had only been kidding about naming Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive Dana White as White House press secretary. He said White loved the idea and that the two would speak on Monday about other matters. For markets, the APEC summit now looms as a significant event, with any progress on Iran carrying implications for oil and any signal on chips bearing directly on Nvidia. body: Traders have largely priced in the political shift. The bigger risk now is to timing: the market structure bill could slip down the agenda while the new majority prioritises investigations. Stablecoin liquidity is the pressure point to watch, because Tether sits at the centre of crypto trading. A memecoin issuer has no such role. The WLFI token and the USD1 stablecoin face the most direct reputational risk from the probe. Bitcoin and ether face only indirect, sentiment-driven exposure. Blumenthal has spent most of a year writing letters to crypto firms; from January his requests come with the power to compel answers. US Senator Richard Blumenthal has given Binance, Tether and two crypto businesses tied to President Donald Trump until January 4, 2027, to hand over outstanding records, and the date matters more than the demand. It falls one day after the new Congress convenes, when Blumenthal is expected to take the chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations following the Democrats’ sweep of both chambers in the November 3 midterms. The letters, announced on November 5, went to Binance, Tether, World Liberty Financial and Fight Fight Fight LLC, the company behind the TRUMP memecoin. World Liberty and Fight Fight Fight were asked to begin producing documents by November 30. Blumenthal warned the subcommittee would look at other ways to secure compliance if the records were not delivered by the January deadline, and coverage of the Democratic sweep has read that as a signal subpoenas could follow. CNN reported that the same round of letters also went to Trump administration officials and several large corporate donors. None of the underlying lines of inquiry is new. Blumenthal opened his investigation into World Liberty Financial and the TRUMP coin in May 2025. In February he pressed Binance over a reported $1.7 billion in Iran-linked transfers, which the exchange disputed, saying its sanctions-related exposure had fallen sharply since early 2024. In October he wrote to Tether over reported payments to a consulting firm co-founded by former White House crypto adviser Bo Hines, which Tether has said involved no wrongdoing, and to Cantor Fitzgerald over its ties to the stablecoin issuer. What has changed is leverage. As the minority’s ranking member, Blumenthal could only ask for voluntary cooperation, and recipients are not obliged to respond until the new Congress is seated. From January, the requests come from a subcommittee chair with the tools to compel documents. For Bitcoin and ether, the direct price impact looks limited for now. The market has already absorbed the larger political shock: Bitcoin briefly fell below $76,000 as results came in on November 4 before recovering, while ether dropped to a two-month low in the same move, according to market reports. The letters target named companies, not the assets themselves. The more plausible channel to prices runs through Washington’s calendar, where an investigations-heavy agenda could compete for time with the stalled CLARITY Act market structure bill. A longer wait for clear US rules would likely weigh on sentiment more than any single letter. Tether is the exception worth watching, because USDT is the largest stablecoin and a core source of trading liquidity, so sustained pressure on its compliance record would touch market plumbing in a way a probe of a memecoin promoter would not. Ether’s sharper election-week drop suggests it has been the more sensitive of the two to US policy risk, though that is an observation from one move rather than a fixed relationship. What to watch next: the first marker is November 30, when World Liberty and Fight Fight Fight are due to start producing records, and a refusal or thin response would make January subpoenas more likely. body: A hot PPI and a soft CPI is a poor mix for China’s growth outlook. It points to margin compression for manufacturers and weak domestic demand, which weighs on sentiment toward Chinese equities and keeps expectations of policy support alive. For the yuan, softer underlying inflation argues for easier policy at the margin, a mild negative. For the Australian dollar and commodity currencies, the read is mixed: firm producer prices reflect cost pressure rather than a demand-led recovery in China’s appetite for raw materials. For oil, the PPI surge mainly shows the energy shock feeding through, not new demand strength. China’s factories are facing their fastest price rises in years while consumer inflation slips further below 1%, a split that points to squeezed margins and fragile domestic demand rather than any healthy reflation. China’s factory-gate inflation accelerated more sharply than expected in October, while consumer price growth slowed below forecasts. The result widens the gap between surging producer costs and weak household demand. The producer price index rose 5.7% from a year earlier, well above expectations of around 5.3% and up from 5% in September, when it had already reached a four-year high. Consumer prices increased 0.7% year-on-year, slightly below the 0.8% forecast and down from 0.9% in September. They were flat on the month, in line with expectations, after a 0.2% gain in September. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, eased to 0.8% from 1%, also undershooting forecasts of 0.9%. The divergence between the two measures has now widened to around five percentage points. Producer prices are being driven higher by energy and other input costs, while consumer prices show little sign of following. That suggests manufacturers and retailers are absorbing much of the cost increase rather than passing it on, a reflection of soft domestic demand and limited pricing power. The core reading is the more telling figure for the health of the domestic economy. A slowdown in underlying inflation to below 1% points to subdued demand for services and non-essential goods, despite some support from spending around the National Day Golden Week holiday at the start of October. For policymakers, the mix is awkward. Weak consumer and core inflation strengthens the case for further support for domestic demand. The jump in producer prices, though, limits room for aggressive easing and squeezes industrial profit margins at a time when firms are already facing higher energy costs linked to the war with Iran. The data come as Beijing is also moving to shore up confidence in its stock market, with a recent State Council meeting calling for stronger capital market stabilisation mechanisms. Attention now turns to October trade data due on Tuesday, which will show whether export strength can continue to offset sluggish domestic demand. Credit and money supply figures follow later in the week. There's always something new to learn about the markets. body: A PPI print above 5% alongside sub-1% CPI would reinforce the market’s read that China is importing cost pressure without the demand to pass it on. That is a negative mix for industrial profits and for confidence in the domestic recovery. A soft CPI reading would keep expectations alive for further policy support from Beijing, which would weigh modestly on the yuan. For commodity-linked currencies such as the Australian dollar, the key signal is demand: weak consumer prices argue against a strong pickup in China’s appetite for raw materials. For oil, firm PPI mainly reflects the energy shock already under way rather than new demand strength. China’s October inflation data is expected to show factory-gate prices racing ahead while consumer prices barely move, a split that points to squeezed margins and fragile domestic demand rather than a healthy reflation. China releases October consumer and producer price data at 01:30 GMT on Monday, 8:30pm US Eastern time on Sunday. Forecasts point to a further widening of the gap between subdued consumer inflation and rapidly rising factory-gate prices. Consumer prices are expected to rise around 0.8% from a year earlier, edging down from 0.9% in September. Forecasts are tightly clustered, with most estimates sitting between 0.7% and 0.9%. Some forecasters see prices unchanged on the month, after a 0.2% rise in September that undershot expectations. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, is projected to hold near 1%. Consumer demand has been subdued but steady. Spending ahead of the National Day Golden Week holiday in early October offered some support, although purchases brought forward before the break diluted its impact on the month as a whole. The producer price index is where the pressure lies. Annual PPI inflation is forecast to rise to around 5.2% to 5.3%, with some estimates higher, from 5% in September, when it hit a four-year high and comfortably beat expectations. Energy costs have been a key driver of the acceleration. Month-on-month gains are expected to slow sharply from September’s pace, but not by enough to stop the annual rate from climbing further. That combination is the central story. Rising producer prices alongside consumer inflation stuck below 1% suggest that manufacturers are absorbing much of the cost increase rather than passing it on to households, a sign of weak pricing power in a soft domestic economy. It also squeezes industrial profit margins. The data open a busy week for China. October trade figures follow on 10 November, after exports surged in September. Money supply, new loans and total social financing are due on 13 November. A CPI print at or below forecast would reinforce the picture of fragile domestic demand. A PPI surprise to the upside would add to concerns over imported cost pressure and keep the focus on how long China’s factories can hold the line on prices. title: Iraq’s 5 Million Bpd Oil Claim Complicates Its OPEC Quota Push

body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar Iraq's campaign for a larger OPEC production allocation has taken a complicated turn after Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said the country is already producing more than 5 million barrels per day , more than half a million barrels above its current OPEC+ requirement. Khudair’s statement raises a basic question over Iraq’s current production as OPEC prepares to set production levels for 2027. Just six days earlier, Baghdad joined six other OPEC+ producers in agreeing to maintain current production requirements for December, leaving Iraq at 4.431 million bpd. Shortly after Khudair put Iraqi production above 5 million bpd, the Oil Ministry reaffirmed Iraq's commitment to the 4.431 million bpd ceiling, saying October production had increased but giving no figure. Baghdad has spent months trying to persuade OPEC to recognize substantially more Iraqi production capacity. Iraq is seeking a future baseline based on capacity of around 6 million bpd, while OPEC is independently assessing members' maximum sustainable production capacity as it prepares its 2027 production framework. Iraq reported production of 4.399 million bpd to OPEC in September, before the Oil Ministry reported a further increase in October without providing a figure. Khudair said Iraq remained compliant with OPEC because its exports were within what he described as the group’s “export ceiling.” But Iraq’s 4.431 million bpd OPEC+ requirement is a production target, not an export target. OPEC’s rules are explicit on this point. Compliance is assessed using crude oil production , based on estimates from independent secondary sources. As Bloomberg’s Javier Blas has explained , OPEC+ has occasionally allowed individual countries to make commitments based partly on exports, most notably Russia, creating an increasingly complicated collection of cuts and targets. But that is not how Iraq’s current 4.431 million bpd requirement is defined: it applies to crude production. For Iraq, exports and production can differ significantly. Crude produced in Iraq can be exported, domestically refined, directly consumed for power generation or moved into storage. Iraq’s OPEC+ requirement, however, is measured against crude production rather than the volume ultimately exported. Related: The Iran War Isn't Over, but Oil Traders Are Already Pricing In Peace That is why Khudair’s explanation does not resolve the problem created by his own production figure. Iraq could export less than 4.431 million bpd and still produce more than its OPEC+ requirement. And if Khudair’s figure of more than 5 million bpd refers to crude production as OPEC defines it, it would put Iraqi output at least 569,000 bpd above the nominal requirement. OPEC does not simply use Baghdad’s reported production number when assessing compliance. It uses estimates from independent secondary sources, and those estimates can differ substantially from Iraq’s own figures. Khudair’s statement therefore does not establish that OPEC itself will record Iraqi production above 5 million bpd. But his reference to exports does not explain how production above that level would comply with Iraq’s production requirement. The U.S.-Iran war has radically changed the relationship between production and exports across the Gulf. For months, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have been producing below their OPEC+ allowances as the closure of Hormuz and continuing shipping disruptions restricted Gulf exports. That raises an obvious question as to whether OPEC has quietly become more interested in how much oil its members can actually export than how much they produce. So far, there is no direct indication that it has. OPEC’s Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC) directly addressed the disruption to international maritime routes in October, but continued to assess members using crude oil production data and adherence to production adjustments. body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… The blue wave in the midterm elections that will put Democrats in charge of the House and Senate could reshape U.S. energy policies. Democrats in charge of both chambers of Congress and its key committees, Democratic governors in key data-center development states such as Ohio, Georgia, and Texas, a Democrat in Georgia’s utilities regulator, and the first Democratic member of the Texas oil regulator since 1990 would seek to stymie the Trump Administration’s pro-fossil fuel and unchecked data center expansion. Investigations into oil deals involving the White House, including “the biggest oil deal in world history” in Venezuela , and the ‘diesel deal’ with Russia’s Vladimir Putin on the eve of the elections are likely to be top of the agenda. Policy uncertainty at the federal level will increase, as Democrats are likely to attempt to bring back some clean energy tax credits. President Donald Trump has vowed to become ‘Mr Veto’ and veto legislation he doesn’t like. The Democratic-majority Congress will need support from Republican lawmakers to overcome a presidential veto, so changes to the energy policy are unlikely to be radical, but rather a compromise. Related: The Iran War Isn't Over, but Oil Traders Are Already Pricing In Peace Executive orders and war powers remain a tool for President Trump, but Congress now controls appropriations and budgets, so both sides will have to make concessions – “deals” in Trump’s parlance – in many key policy areas, including energy. A Democratic-controlled Congress could push for regulation of AI, while governors from Texas to Ohio could halt the expansion plans amid concerns about how soaring power demand from AI would hit household bills. No wonder tech stocks crashed on Wednesday as most results of the midterm elections showed stunning victories in many key-race states. Investigations are coming, Democratic Senator Ed of Massachusetts said on election night. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” said Markey, who is on the environment and public works committee. In Texas, oil and gas engineer Jon Rosenthal won the open seat on the three-member Texas Railroad Commission, becoming the first Democrat on the commission since 1990. Rosenthal will be in the minority, but could influence some issues, including data center permitting and wastewater disposal from oil and gas production. The war in Iran is the biggest international issue that Congress will face, and that will influence international oil prices and U.S. fuel prices in the coming months. Analysts still believe there is currently more chance of a U.S. escalation rather than de-escalation in Iran, but the Democratic Congress, as of January 1, could pressure Trump into reaching a deal. “With war funding and appointees now subject to a hostile majority, the administration faces greater institutional pressure to pursue a Hormuz deal rather than a further round of strikes,” analysts at Rystad Energy said on the day after the elections. “A restoration of flows through the Strait of Hormuz is the prerequisite for Middle East crude supply and refined product inventories to normalize,” they noted. U.S. voters showed that the cost of living and the cost of gasoline top their concerns and punished the Administration, whose war on Iran drove fuel prices to record highs for this time of year. The first sign of whether compromises between the executive and legislative branches could work will be seen as early as November 9, when a proposed bipartisan permitting bill is scheduled for a procedural vote in the Senate. body: Producer prices in China grew at the fastest rate since June 2022, accelerating for the third month in a row. The PPI for October came in at 5.7%, compared to the 5.3% expected by economists polled by Reuters. Consumer inflation in China slowed to 0.7% in October, its first deceleration after two straight months of increases. The figure missed expectations of a 0.8% rise from economists polled by Reuters, and was lower than the 0.9% seen in September. The Chinese economy has shown some signs of expansion recently. It grew faster than expected in the third quarter, and September saw a sharp beat in retail sales.

title: US Inflation Concerns Deepen as Missing BLS Data Complicates Economic Outlook - Tekedia
body: Inflation remains one of the biggest economic concerns in the United States, with Federal Reserve officials, bond investors and frustrated voters increasingly sharing the view that rising prices are still too high and may remain elevated for longer than expected. Despite previous efforts to bring inflation under control, the cost of living continues to influence household spending, financial markets and expectations about the direction of monetary policy. However, understanding the true state of inflation has become more complicated because of gaps in the government’s economic data collection. Join Tekedia Capital Syndicate and co-invest in great global startups. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) , responsible for producing some of the country’s most important inflation indicators, faced an extraordinary disruption last fall when it could not collect sufficient information for most of October’s inflation report. The interruption created the first monthly gap in the headline inflation series, leaving policymakers, investors and economists without a complete picture of price movements during a particularly important period. The development highlights how dependent American economy is on reliable government statistics. Inflation measurements influence everything from Federal Reserve interest-rate decisions and Treasury bond yields to wage negotiations, pension adjustments and business investment plans. When the data becomes unavailable, economic decision-making becomes considerably more difficult. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is among the most closely watched indicators because it measures changes in the prices consumers pay for goods and services. It provides insight into how quickly household expenses are increasing and whether monetary policy is successfully reducing inflationary pressure. Collecting accurate CPI information requires extensive surveys, price observations and consistent statistical procedures. Without October’s complete information, economists faced difficulties determining whether inflationary pressures were accelerating, slowing or simply remaining unchanged. Missing observations complicate comparisons between monthly reports, potentially creating uncertainty around the underlying direction of prices. For the Federal Reserve, the timing could hardly be more sensitive. The central bank must balance its responsibility to maintain price stability with the need to support employment and economic growth. If inflation remains stubbornly high, policymakers may have to maintain restrictive interest rates for longer. Conversely, evidence of sustained disinflation could strengthen arguments for monetary easing. Bond investors are sensitive to these developments because inflation expectations influence Treasury yields and the anticipated path of interest rates. Persistent inflation generally increases the likelihood that borrowing costs will remain elevated, putting pressure on government financing, mortgages, corporate borrowing and equity valuations. American households have reasons to remain concerned. Even when inflation slows, prices rarely return to their previous levels. Consumers therefore continue experiencing the cumulative effects of earlier increases in housing, food, transportation, healthcare and other essential expenses. The missing October report introduces another challenge: separating genuine changes in inflation from uncertainty created by incomplete measurements. Economists may need to rely more heavily on alternative indicators. including private-sector surveys, industry pricing information and other government statistics. The disruption demonstrates that controlling inflation requires more than interest-rate adjustments. It depends on accurate, timely economic information. Without dependable measurements, policymakers risk making decisions based on an incomplete understanding of economic conditions. title: Goldman Sachs Cuts Gold Price Forecasts as Hawkish Federal Reserve Weighs on Demand - Yahoo Finance
body: Goldman Sachs has lowered its gold price forecasts for the end of 2026 and 2027, citing the Federal Reserve's increasingly hawkish monetary policy stance and its impact on investor demand. However, the investment bank maintained a positive longer-term outlook, supported by substantial central bank purchases. Strategists led by Lina Thomas reduced their end-2026 gold price target to $4,150 per ounce from $4,650. The forecast for the end of 2027 was lowered to $4,800 per ounce from $5,400. The revised projections assume that the Fed's tighter policy stance, including an anticipated interest rate increase in December, will limit demand for gold as protection against currency depreciation and broader economic policy risks. Goldman expects investor demand for gold as a hedge against monetary and fiscal uncertainty to return toward historical averages rather than revisit the elevated levels recorded earlier in 2026. The bank compared current market conditions with 2022, when strong central bank purchases supported gold prices but higher interest rates limited investment demand. Higher borrowing costs generally reduce the attractiveness of gold because the precious metal does not generate interest income. Goldman also expects demand for gold call options, which can reflect investor interest in protection against policy-related risks, to moderate. Despite reducing its near-term forecasts, Goldman continues to view central bank demand as a significant structural driver of gold prices. The bank expects central banks to purchase approximately 60 tonnes of gold per month throughout 2026 and 2027, substantially above the average of 17 tonnes recorded before 2022. Its latest estimate places current purchases at approximately 85 tonnes per month, based on a seasonally adjusted three-month average. "We retain our longer-term constructive view on structurally strong central bank demand – which drives most of the 15% price upside we forecast by end-2027," the strategists wrote. Goldman noted that emerging-market central banks, particularly China, continue to hold relatively low gold allocations compared with potential long-term reserve targets. Developed-market central banks have generally participated less in the recent purchasing trend, partly because they already maintain substantial historical gold reserves. "But the debate is increasingly shifting from whether to own gold to where to store it, pointing to broader concerns around reserve security and cross-country trust," the strategists added. Goldman expects gold prices to receive additional support when the Federal Reserve begins reducing interest rates. The bank's economists anticipate rate cuts beginning in late 2027 and continuing into early 2028, potentially easing pressure on gold and encouraging renewed private investment demand. For shorter-term investors, however, the outlook remains challenging. Goldman identified rising interest rates, uncertain energy prices and restrictive risk limits as potential obstacles for commodity trading advisers and macro hedge funds over the next three to six months. Higher oil prices could also trigger additional selling by systematic investment strategies. The bank warned that gold could face further downward pressure if the Fed raises rates again in March 2027, delays monetary easing or increases its projected terminal interest rate. Under that scenario, Goldman estimates gold could reach $4,660 per ounce by the end of 2027, below its revised base-case forecast of $4,800. Conversely, renewed concerns about government debt sustainability and fiscal policy could increase demand for gold as a hedge, potentially pushing prices above the bank's central forecast. Goldman suggested that longer-term investors seeking exposure to sustained central bank purchases or protection against economic policy risks may view the current correction as a potential entry opportunity.

title: Bank of England raises interest rates, signals further hikes - Big News Network.com
body: LONDON, U.K.: The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4 percent on November 5, its first increase in more than three years, warning that further tightening could be necessary as the US-Iran conflict continues to drive up energy costs and threaten Britain's inflation outlook. The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to increase its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point from 3.75 percent. The lone dissenter, Catherine Mann, supported a larger half-point increase to 4.25 percent. The decision comes as the bank forecasts inflation will reach approximately 5 percent by the middle of next year, more than twice its 2 percent target, creating further cost-of-living challenges for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government. "Today's increase shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase," Governor Andrew Bailey said. Although the bank has seen limited evidence of accelerating inflation outside sectors directly affected by higher energy costs, policymakers concluded that months of elevated prices had created sufficient future inflationary pressure to justify immediate action. Consumer price inflation reached 3.5 percent in September, raising concerns among some policymakers that inflation expectations could become harder to control. Mann, who had previously criticised the bank for being too slow to reassure markets about inflation, cited "non-linear inflation risks" and warned of a possible loss of confidence in the central bank. Financial markets had widely anticipated Thursday's increase and were pricing in three further quarter-point hikes during 2027, more than most economists expect. Bailey said the difference reflected financial markets accounting for the possibility of a sharper rise in energy prices, while economists generally based their forecasts on a more moderate tightening cycle. "Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates," he said in the policy minutes. Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli also indicated that another increase would probably be needed in the near term. External policymaker Megan Greene called for "further tightening", while Chief Economist Huw Pill referred to the need for "additional hikes". However, policymakers Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor said they would require stronger evidence of secondary inflationary effects before supporting additional increases. Alongside the rate decision, the Bank of England upgraded its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to 1.6 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, exceeding projections issued by the government's Office for Budget Responsibility last week. The bank attributed some of the stronger outlook to investment in artificial intelligence and a modest temporary boost from Finance Minister John Healey's annual budget. Under its central forecast, inflation is expected to peak at an average of 4.8 percent in the second quarter of 2027. In a more adverse scenario, with oil prices reaching approximately $130 a barrel instead of around $100, inflation could climb to 6.2 percent in the third quarter of 2027. The bank now expects inflation to return to its 2 percent target only in the third quarter of 2028, six months later than it projected in July. It also forecast that British households' income from work, after accounting for inflation and taxes, would decline both this year and next. The government's latest budget is expected to reduce inflation by 0.25 percentage points at its peak, although the bank warned that inflation could rise again when temporary cost-of-living support measures expire.

WTI ( USOIL ) crude oil rose about 4.3% to around $92.7; Brent ( UKOIL ) crude oil rose about 4.2%, breaking above $105. With the US and Iran yet to reach an agreement to end the conflict, combined with potential US reassessment of military options against Iran, the market rapidly priced in a crude supply disruption risk premium. Gold ( XAUUSD ) fluctuated near $4,120, as geopolitical safe-haven demand was offset by a stronger US dollar and rising Treasury yields. In cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin ( BTC ) fell about 1%, trading near $82,500. Rising oil prices and expectations of further Fed rate hikes weakened demand for highly volatile risk assets. Palantir ( PLTR ) rose about 2.4% in pre-market trading. Goldman Sachs ( GS ) upgraded Palantir from Neutral to Buy with a price target of $230; Yorkville Ives also assigned an Outperform rating and a $250 price target, believing sovereign AI and enterprise AI demand will continue to expand the company's addressable market. ExxonMobil ( XOM ) rose about 2.1% in pre-market trading. A rapid rise in international oil prices boosted earnings expectations for upstream energy companies; Chevron ( CVX ) also rose about 2.2% in pre-market trading. PepsiCo ( PEP ) rose about 2% in pre-market trading. The company's third-quarter revenue grew 5.6% year-over-year to $25.27 billion, beating market expectations of $24.95 billion; adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.34, also better than expected. However, the company lowered its full-year adjusted EPS growth guidance from 5%-7% to 2.5%-3.5%. Intel ( INTC ) fell about 2.5% in pre-market trading. The market continues to focus on Intel's specific role in Elon Musk's Terafab AI chip factory plan, while chip stocks generally faced profit-taking pressure following rising U.S. Treasury yields and recent sharp gains. TSMC ( TSM ) ADR fell about 1.6% in pre-market trading. TSMC reported September revenue of NT$511.86 billion, up 54.6% year-over-year; cumulative revenue in the first nine months of this year grew 41.1%. Although AI chip demand remains strong, pressure from high interest rates and a broader pullback in the semiconductor sector weighed on the stock price. The US and Iran have not reached an agreement to end the conflict. According to The Associated Press citing The Atlantic, the White House has asked the Pentagon to study options for striking Iran ahead of the November midterm elections. The report cited two anonymous officials, and the action plans have not been officially confirmed. Federal Reserve officials continued to signal rate hikes. Minutes of the September meeting showed that a majority of officials believed another rate hike before the end of the year could be appropriate; Fed Governor Waller said Thursday he expects further rate hikes will be needed if economic data continues to meet expectations, but hikes do not need to be consecutive.

Set us as preferred Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, leader of one of the world’s hottest chipmakers , is under immense scrutiny after he admitted to an extramarital affair, and the company’s board said it plans to investigate him in light of recent reporting that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The stunning admission follows an investigation by the New York Times that reported that Nvidia’s leader was targeted by former Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, who the U.S. government suspects was recruited by a Chinese spy agency. The CEO previously denied having anything but a “normal” relationship with the woman. Analysts say this will prompt calls for closer examination of tech companies’ dealings with China. “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” said Daniel Ives, partner and senior managing director at merchant bank Yorkville Ives & Co. in an equity research note. “This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC,” wrote Ives, who has an “outperform” rating on the stock. Nvidia’s board said in a statement on Sunday that it has confidence in Huang and his leadership team. On Sunday in after-hours trading, Nvidia’s stock was $188.70 a share, up about 1%. Santa Clara chipmaker Nvidia has ridden the AI revolution to briefly vault over Microsoft and Apple and become the world’s most valuable company. “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” Nvidia’s board said. In a staff memo, Huang apologized to his family and Nvidia employees. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang wrote that he is committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security, adding that he is “proud and grateful to be an American” and supports the investigation. The transgression blemishes Huang’s leadership, which has been admired by many people in Silicon Valley. Huang, a former microprocessor designer and Denny’s dishwasher, discussed the idea behind Nvidia inside a Denny’s in San Jose with fellow entrepreneurs Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. They co-founded the Santa Clara-based chipmaker in 1993. Since then, Huang’s profile has risen to the status of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, with thousands of people gathering to hear his keynotes. The company’s valuation has risen dramatically in recent years alongside AI’s boom. The company reached a record market capitalization of nearly $5.8 trillion in October. That has slipped below $5 trillion, however, weighed down by concern about the sustainability of AI infrastructure build-out. Nvidia became the first publicly traded company to reach a market cap of $4 trillion last week, as investors remain bullish on artificial intelligence technology. “It certainly is going to put a cloud over Jensen and Nvidia for a while,” said Rob Enderle, principal analyst at advisory services firm Enderle Group, adding that Nvidia sells products to the U.S. Department of Defense. “If it turns out that he was intimate with the Chinese spy, Nvidia could face some pullback from the U.S. government.” The company has no public succession plan, and Huang has no obvious heir apparent. He has repeatedly said he wants to continue in his role for decades and has created an informal organizational structure around him that eschews a conventional hierarchy. body: Semiconductor stocks plunged after the U.S. midterm elections in which the Democratic Party scored a landslide, but brokerages said the market's fears are overdone. Concerns grew that the Democrats' victory could delay data center construction in the United States, but many facilities have already broken ground and demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing remains solid. Kim Jae-seung of Hyundai Motor Securities said in a report on the 9th, "We believe the market overreacted relative to fundamentals after the Democratic blue wave, as investor sentiment toward AI had already weakened and the Democrats' bigger-than-expected win spooked the market." In the U.S. midterm elections held on the 3rd, the Democratic Party took control of both the House and the Senate. In particular, Democratic candidates performed unexpectedly well in Republican strongholds such as Texas, turning what had been called a "blue wave (Democratic win)" into a "blue tsunami (Democratic landslide)." What the stock market reacted to most sensitively were the gubernatorial races. State governments and local governments in the United States can influence new data center construction permits, approvals to connect to the power grid, and land use. With the Democrats' victory, expectations spread that approvals for new data centers would become stricter and construction timelines could be delayed. Since the 3rd, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has plunged 11.4%. The KOSPI, where semiconductor stocks carry significant weight, and Taiwan's Taiex fell 10.4% and 8.3%, respectively. The declines were steeper than the Dow Jones Industrial Average (-1.0%) and the Standard & Poor's (S&P) 500 (-2.5%) over the same period. Selling was concentrated in semiconductor-related stocks rather than reflecting a broad-based global market drop. However, the actual impact on data center construction was expected to be limited. Because President Trump can exercise a veto, it will be difficult for a Democrat-controlled Congress to tighten regulations, and regulations at the level of State Governments are also more likely to focus on new projects than on facilities that have already broken ground. A survey by U.S. semiconductor industry analysis firm SemiAnalysis on the 1st of this month found that about 75% of the 33.8 gigawatts (GW) of net new data center capacity scheduled to come online next year across 20 major states had already broken ground. Even if approvals for new projects are delayed, the effect on next year's data center supply may be limited. However, Kim noted, "Many data centers scheduled to come online in 2028 have not yet broken ground, and since planned capacity in Texas accounts for about 29% of the U.S. total, uncertainty around new projects could persist." Data centers' contributions to local economies were also cited as a factor lowering the likelihood of tougher regulations. Loudoun County, Virginia, which has a high concentration of data centers in the United States, collected $1.2 billion in data center-related taxes in fiscal year 2026. That amounts to 39% of the overall budget. Analysts said it would be hard for State Governments and local governments to overlook the tax revenue and jobs that data centers generate. Kim said, "For big tech companies, it could be advantageous to move up the start date even if that means bearing higher costs." He said data center operators could find common ground with local communities by shouldering additional expenses such as electricity and water costs. Analysts also said the main reason Republicans lost the U.S. midterms had more to do with economic issues, including household cost burdens, than with data centers. With both the Democratic Party and the Trump administration likely to focus on stabilizing prices and energy costs over the next two years, policy may lean toward expanding cost sharing with local communities rather than restricting data center construction itself.
